aisle

/EYEL/ - sounds exactly like isle and I'll · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Aisle means a passageway between rows, such as rows of seats or store shelves.

Marco pushed the cart down the cereal aisle twice before admitting he was lost in the unfamiliar grocery store.

Worked Example

When the museum rearranged its gift shop, the fire marshal made the owners widen every aisle: wheelchairs, she explained, need a clear passage between the shelves, and in an emergency a blocked aisle becomes a trap.

Aisle is more exact than 'path' or 'space' because it names the walking passage between rows — of seats, shelves, or pews — a corridor without walls, defined only by what stands on either side of it.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

walkway: A walkway is a built path — boardwalk planks, a paved strip, a covered bridge between buildings — laid down to carry walkers from one place to another. An aisle is not built at all: it is the clear passage left between rows, defined only by the seats or shelves standing on either side.

gangway: A gangway is a boarding passage — the ramp or plank passengers cross to get onto a ship — or a way shouted clear through a crowd. An aisle already runs inside, threading between the rows; a gangway is about getting aboard or getting through in the first place.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

barricade: a barrier thrown up to stop movement — the opposite of a passage kept clear

blockage: anything jamming a passage shut

Where it sits · how big and purposeful the opening is — gap → aisle → concourse

gap vs. aisle: A gap is any opening at all — two boxes shoved apart make one — while an aisle is a purposeful passage, kept clear so people can move along the rows.

concourse vs. aisle: A concourse outgrows an aisle entirely: where an aisle threads between rows of seats or shelves, a station concourse is a hall wide enough to swallow a whole crowd at once.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — aisle

Root — aisle: a wing of a building (from Latin ala, wing)

Put it together

Put it together: There is nothing to peel off here: aisle came into English whole. Latin ala ('wing') named the side sections of a church — the 'wings' flanking the central seating — and Old French wore it down to ele. English then respelled it under the influence of French aile and of the unrelated word isle, which is how a silent s crept into a word that never had one.

Why there's no relative to spot

Why there's no relative to spot: Aisle is a whole-word borrowing: Latin ala ('wing') became Old French ele, and English dressed it in the spelling of the unrelated isle. The wing-root built no other everyday English word, so the spelling — silent s and all — simply has to be memorized.

Strength Check

Word Choice

neutral / everyday

Aisle is the exact word for the passage between rows — theater seats, supermarket shelves, church pews, airplane seats. A corridor runs between walls and a walkway can go anywhere, but the moment rows line both sides, aisle is the word English reaches for. Spell it with care: the s is silent, borrowed from isle, an unrelated word.
